audit.structure: Markdown with ## section headers, single big template literal in agent.ts:330-358. Delivered as the `system` role string. Fixed top-to-bottom order: (1) identity sentence, (2) ## Background, (3) ## Personality, (4) ## Your deepest drives, (5) ## Speech style, (6) ## Current state (Location/Activity/Mood), (7) roleDirective: ## What you know → module role section → ## People you know → ## What drives you right now, (8) stressGrowthBlock, (9) ## Your memories, (10) optional ## Your secret, (11) optional ## Your inner conflict, (12) additionalContext (player-chat: secrets→trust→approach→IL), (13) ## Rules. User message is a separate role (the player/NPC utterance; multi-turn history passed via `history` for chatStream). Roughly the same string is then EITHER sent to LM Studio as system, OR passed to `claude -p --system-prompt` (full replacement of Claude Code's own prompt) where the cwd CLAUDE.local.md persona file is layered on top via Claude Code memory autoload. Two routes = two assemblies stacked for the claude-code case.

audit.limitsAndTruncation: Memories: recall() top-5 by relevance (hard-coded 5 in chat/chatStream/generateResponse), labeled by decayed importance. Beliefs in ## What you know: top-3 (summarizeForPrompt maxBeliefs=3, sliced AFTER filtering object/subject != null — NOT sorted by confidence here, relies on getAllBeliefs order). Crime-justice role builder sorts crimeBeliefs by confidence and takes [0] only. Relationships: filtered to |sentiment|>0.15 OR trust>0.5, no top-N cap. CLAUDE.local.md beliefs.md @-import: top-30 by composite score confidence×recency (serializeMemoryState beliefsTopN=30). maxTokens default 250 (response cap, terse). Chat history kept to last 12 messages (6 exchanges). No summarization of the system prompt itself — it grows unboundedly with directive count (multiple HIDDEN sections can stack). No relevance ranking across the directive sections — they are concatenated in registration order.
qualityRisks: Personality is fragile: bigFiveToDescription emits NOTHING for any trait in 0.3-0.7 (the middle). An NPC with all-moderate traits gets literally 'You are balanced personality.' Mid-range nuance is lost — only extremes are expressed.

Honesty trait: in agent.ts prompt it is folded into the same flat adjective list ('shrewd and self-serving' / 'sincere and fair-minded') with no emphasis, while the parallel CLAUDE.local.md gives it a bold LOW/MID/HIGH lie-willingness tag. Inconsistent salience of a behavior-critical trait between the two routes.

TWO divergent persona representations depending on LLM route (lm-studio vs claude-code). On claude-code, the NPC receives BOTH the prose buildSystemPrompt (as --system-prompt) AND the numeric CLAUDE.local.md persona (autoloaded) — risk of redundancy/conflict (e.g. prose 'calm' vs numeric neuroticism 0.65). On lm-studio it receives only the prose. Behavior is not guaranteed consistent across the toggle.
Duplicated stress/growth tables (agent.ts long vs personality-prose.ts short) — drift risk; the short ones are dead/used elsewhere, easy to edit the wrong copy.

## Rules bullet 'Reply in the SAME language the player speaks; never mix languages' assumes a language-detection the model must do itself; with a Russian-speaking player and English-only persona/background/secret prose, this invites code-switching or instruction conflict.

No few-shot examples in the player-chat system prompt: speechStyle 'Example:' lines are passed raw (no rotation) so the model can copy them verbatim — the anti-copy rotation in speechReminder() is NOT applied on this path, only in NPC-NPC conversation/interaction.

Self-name rule is phrased as 'Never refer to yourself by your own name. Always use I/me/my — never "${name}".' This is a documented known issue (name hallucination) and a single negative instruction is weak for small models (Qwen 9B).

Over-stuffing: when an NPC simultaneously has a secret, inner conflict, a HIDDEN crime directive, a heat directive, a trust directive, role duty, stress prose, beliefs and relationships, the system prompt becomes a long wall of competing imperatives — the 9B 'lost in the middle' problem is acknowledged in code (shop items moved to user message at server.ts:299) but the equally-buried secret/role directives are NOT given the same treatment.

Mutually-exclusive role directive: only the FIRST matching branch fires (investigator else perpetrator else witness else unease). An investigator who is ALSO a perpetrator only ever gets ACTIVE DUTY framing — guilt is silently dropped.

Mood prose and stress/growth prose can contradict: moodDescription at mood<-0.5 says 'deeply shaken, voice flat' while the same mood triggers e.g. stressType 8 'domineering and confrontational' — the two SHARED tables aren't reconciled.

Beliefs ## What you know is NOT confidence-sorted before slice(3) — order depends on getAllBeliefs() insertion order, so the 3 shown may not be the most certain/important ones (contrast with the role builder and the top-30 file path which DO sort).
buildHeatDirective uses literal fallback 'your victim' / affectedName 'someone' when names unresolved — can surface vague pronouns into otherwise specific prose.

The CLAUDE.local.md builder docstrings/comments still say 'CLAUDE.md' though the file is actually CLAUDE.local.md — cosmetic, but the prose persona 'How I respond' rules partly duplicate the agent.ts ## Rules with slightly different wording (e.g. 'never acknowledge being an AI' exists in CLAUDE.local.md but NOT in agent.ts Rules), so anti-AI-disclosure is route-dependent.
No explicit instruction bounding response length in tokens beyond 'Keep responses concise' + maxTokens 250 hard cut — mid-sentence truncation possible for verbose NPCs.
improvementIdeas: Make bigFiveToDescription emit graded descriptors for the 0.3-0.7 band (e.g. 'moderately outgoing') or at minimum surface raw scores, so middle-of-the-road NPCs aren't flattened to 'balanced personality'.

Unify the two persona representations: either always include the numeric OCEAN+H block (with the LOW/MID/HIGH honesty tag) in buildSystemPrompt too, or drop the prose duplication on the claude-code route — pick one source of truth so behavior doesn't shift with the LLM toggle.
Delete or merge the duplicated short stress/growth tables in personality-prose.ts (or have agent.ts import from one canonical table) to kill drift risk.

Sort beliefs by confidence (or the composite score already used in serializeMemoryState) before slice(3) in beliefs.summarizeForPrompt so the 3 shown are the 3 most important, matching the file-based path.

Apply the same 'lost middle' mitigation used for shop items to the highest-priority directive (active HIDDEN crime / heat EXTREME DANGER): echo a one-line reminder into the user turn, or move Rules+top-directive to the END of the system prompt.
Add 1-2 short in-character few-shot example exchanges (using the rotated speechReminder example, not the raw verbatim line) to anchor tone for the 9B model.
Reconcile mood vs stress/growth prose: when stress directive fires, suppress or soften the contradictory moodDescription clause, or fold them into a single coherent 'current emotional state' block.

Reframe negative self-name rule as positive guidance plus the model's own pronoun, and consider stripping the NPC's name from the assistant-visible portion entirely, since negative instructions are weak for small models.
Let the role directive accumulate compatible facets (investigator AND perpetrator) instead of first-match-wins, or at least order branches by narrative priority and allow guilt to coexist with duty.

Localize the SHARED boilerplate (Rules, mood, drives) or template the language instruction with the actual detected player language rather than relying on the model to self-detect, given Russian-player / English-persona mismatch.
Add 'never acknowledge being an AI / never break character about being fictional' to the agent.ts ## Rules so the protection isn't claude-code-route-only.

audit.site: CLWA — Beliefs & Vector-Memory → LLM context injection
contentPieces: Belief structured fields (beliefs.ts:6-26): eventType, subject (who did it / null), object (who to / null), location, confidence 0-1, source, sourceNpcId, gameDay, lastUpdated. NL phrasing is generated on the fly — beliefs are never stored as text.

summarizeForPrompt (beliefs.ts:121) — 2nd person belief lines for the live LLM prompt. Default maxBeliefs=3. Filters to beliefs where object!=null OR subject!=null. Certainty prefix by confidence (>0.8 'certain', >0.5 'believe', else 'heard rumor'). Source label suffix. Drops beliefs whose eventType has no registered label (verb null → null → filtered).

summarizeForMemory (beliefs.ts:147) — 3rd person, stored INTO another NPC's memory after a conversation. Default maxBeliefs=2 (callers pass 1). Certainty prefix ('is convinced' >0.7 / 'believes' >0.4 / 'has heard'). Optional eventTypeFilter matching conversation topic; falls back to top-by-confidence if filter empties.

phraseBelief (event-registry.ts:766) — engine scaffolding + module-registered relational verb framing. Crime module registers ONE unconditional phrasing: target!=null ? `${who} committed ${verb} against ${target}` : `${who} committed ${verb}` (crime-justice/index.ts:643). Engine neutral fallback: `${who} — ${verb} (${target})`.

Event labels (verbs) registered by crime module (index.ts:174): NPC_KILLED→'murder', GOODS_STOLEN→'theft', SELF_JUSTICE→'attack', plus ~20 more. getEventLabel returns null for unregistered types → belief silently dropped from prompt.

Belief source labels (index.ts:283): witness→'saw it happen', interrogation→'testimony under questioning', gossip→'hearsay', perpetrator→'committed the act', cover_up→'covering up', secret→'personal knowledge', body_discovery→'found the body', evidence→'physical evidence', deduction→'deduced from clues'.

Ordering: getAllBeliefs (beliefs.ts:117) sorts strictly by confidence DESC, then slice top-N. No recency, no salience, no topic relevance for the main prompt path (summarizeForPrompt). Only summarizeForMemory has optional eventType topic filter.

Role directive builder (crime-justice/index.ts:651) — re-reads beliefs separately (confidence>=0.3, isTransferable) to emit '## ACTIVE DUTY' (investigator), '## How you feel right now' (perpetrator guilt / firsthand witness / generic unease, branched on neuroticism>0.6), and '## Your situation' wanted-fugitive. This duplicates belief content already in the '## What you know' block.

Vector memory (memory.ts) — text experiences embedded via LM Studio, dual-write to _memoryLog (truth) + Qdrant (index). recall() returns ScoredMemory with composite score relevance*0.4 + decayedImportance*0.4 + freshness*0.2 (memory.ts:177). 3-level fallback: Qdrant → cosine brute force → keyword. topK default 5.

Recalled-memory injection (agent.ts:305 buildSystemPrompt): each memory rendered as `- (${timeLabel}, ${vividness}) ${m.text}` under '## Your memories (most relevant to this conversation)'. timeLabel = today/yesterday/N days ago. vividness from decayedImportance (>=7 'vivid', >=4 'clear', else 'fading'). Empty → 'No relevant memories.'
decayedImportance = importance * exp(-daysPassed/(importance*5)); freshness = 1/(daysPassed+1) (decay.ts:8-18). High-importance memories decay slower.

Belief query for recall is the player's raw message / the goal prompt text (agent.ts chat/generateResponse: recall(userMessage|prompt, currentDay, 5)). Autonomous decisions (volition.ts) do NOT recall vector memories — they only get summarizeForPrompt beliefs + relationships.

Conversation-driven belief seeding (interaction.ts:108-114): target NPC observes `${initiator.name} came to talk about ${purposeShort}.${initiatorBeliefs3p}.` — a 3rd-person belief summary (maxBeliefs=1) becomes a new stored memory, so beliefs propagate into the memory store as text.
audit.structure: Two parallel channels feed the LLM. (A) BELIEFS — always-on, structured→NL at prompt-build time. In the autonomous decision path (volition.ts:403) they appear in the USER prompt under 'WHAT YOU KNOW:' (deliberately in user, not system, to avoid lost-in-the-middle, comment at volition.ts:540). In the conversational path (agent.ts buildSystemPrompt → buildRoleDirective, agent.ts:362) they appear in the SYSTEM prompt as '## What you know' plus module role-directive sections ('## ACTIVE DUTY', '## How you feel right now', '## Your situation'). In interaction.ts they are appended as additionalContext '## What you know (facts, not speculation):' for both speakers, and as short 'What you know:'/'What you already know:' lines in the purpose/response prompts. (B) MEMORY — vector-recalled per turn, injected only in the SYSTEM prompt block '## Your memories (most relevant to this conversation)'. System prompt order: name/role → Background → Personality → drives (fear/desire) → Speech style → Current state (location/mood) → roleDirective(beliefs+role+relationships+motive) → stress/growth → memories → secret → inner conflict → additionalContext → Rules. NL phrasing layered: engine certainty prefix + module verb framing (phraseBelief) + engine source-label suffix + optional location.
audit.perNpcVsShared: Per-NPC authored data: profile.name/role/background/personality(bigFive)/enneagram(coreFear,coreDesire)/speechStyle/secret/innerConflict, and the NPC's own beliefs + memory log (emergent, not authored). Shared/hardcoded boilerplate: all wrapper headings ('## What you know', '## Your memories...', 'WHAT YOU KNOW:'), the certainty/vividness ladders, the Rules block, mood prose ladders, and 'No relevant memories.' fallback — identical for every NPC. Module-owned (crime-justice, shared across all crime NPCs): the verb labels, source labels, the single belief-phrasing function ('committed X against Y'), and the role-directive guilt/duty/witness prose (branched only on neuroticism>0.6). Engine stays genre-neutral; crime framing all lives in the module registry (INV-14).
audit.limitsAndTruncation: Beliefs: top-N by confidence only. summarizeForPrompt default N=3 (callers: 3 for decision/role/interaction-context, 2 for purpose/response lines, 3 in il.ts question-handler). summarizeForMemory default N=2 but every caller passes 1. Role-directive builder uses confidence>=0.3 cutoff and picks just the single top belief per branch. Memory recall: Qdrant fetches topK*3 (=15) candidates, re-ranked by composite score, sliced to topK=5 everywhere. Conversation purpose text truncated to 60 chars (interaction.ts) / 50 chars (goals.ts) before storage. Interaction dialogue capped at maxTokens 100 and '15 words'. No global token budget on the assembled prompt; no dedup across the '## What you know' block and the role-directive sections (same belief can appear twice). Beliefs with unregistered eventType labels are dropped entirely (filter(Boolean)).
qualityRisks: No salience/recency/topic ranking for beliefs in the main path — selection is pure confidence DESC (beliefs.ts:117,124). A high-confidence but stale or contextually irrelevant belief always beats a fresh, on-topic, lower-confidence one. Topic relevance exists ONLY in summarizeForMemory's optional eventTypeFilter, not in the prompt-facing summarizeForPrompt.

Stale beliefs: decay floors confidence at 0.1 (beliefs.ts:102) and never deletes. A months-old rumor still surfaces as '- You heard rumor: X committed murder...(hearsay)' competing for the top-3 slots. summarizeForPrompt has no recency cutoff and no 'how long ago' marker, so the LLM cannot tell a fresh belief from a faded one (unlike memories, which carry a timeLabel+vividness).

Belief duplication in the conversational system prompt: '## What you know' (summarizeForPrompt) and the crime role-directive ('## ACTIVE DUTY' / '## How you feel right now') both render the same top belief in different words, wasting context and risking the model treating one incident as two.

Awkward / model-fragile phrasing: 'committed murder against {target}' is grammatically off for theft/attack ('committed theft against Bess', 'committed attack against Bess'). The certainty+phrasing concatenation yields stilted lines like '- You heard rumor: someone unknown committed theft against someone (hearsay)'. The neutral engine fallback '{who} — {verb} ({target})' is near-unreadable if any belief slips through with an unlabeled-but-present verb path.

Silent belief loss: getEventLabel returns null for any unregistered eventType, and summarizeForPrompt maps it to null then filters it out (beliefs.ts:132,139) with no warning — an NPC can 'know' something that never reaches the prompt. Contrast getEventLabelSafe used elsewhere which at least warns.

Vivid/clear/fading vividness label is driven by decayedImportance thresholds (>=7 / >=4) but importance is an authored/heuristic 0-8ish scale; many memories will read 'fading' immediately, and the composite recall score that actually ordered them is invisible to the model, so ordering and stated vividness can disagree.

Recall query is the raw player message or goal prompt (agent.ts:77,201). For terse inputs ('hi', 'what?') the embedding is near-meaningless, so semantic recall returns noise; keyword fallback then needs words >3 chars (memory.ts:203) and silently returns nothing for short queries.

Autonomous decisions never recall episodic memory (volition.ts only uses beliefs+relationships) — an NPC's vivid lived experiences do not inform its tick-to-tick choices, only its conversation replies. Possible intentional split, but a real asymmetry in what the LLM 'remembers' when acting vs speaking.

Beliefs-as-memory feedback loop: interaction.ts:112 stores a 3rd-person belief summary as a new memory ('Mark came to talk about ... Mark is convinced X committed murder against Y'). That text later re-embeds and re-surfaces via recall, so a belief can echo back as a 'memory', compounding any phrasing oddity and potentially reinforcing stale info.

No cap on combined prompt size — beliefs + role directives + relationships + 5 memories + secret + inner-conflict + background all concatenate unbounded; long backgrounds/secrets can push the (already low-priority, bottom-of-prompt) memory block toward truncation by the local 9B model.
improvementIdeas: Add recency/salience to summarizeForPrompt ranking instead of pure confidence: reuse the memory composite idea (confidence * w1 + freshness(currentDay-lastUpdated) * w2), and/or pass the current topic/eventType so prompt beliefs can be topic-filtered the way summarizeForMemory already optionally is.

Emit a recency cue on belief lines (mirror the memory 'today/yesterday/N days ago' + vivid/clear/fading), so the LLM can weight a faded rumor below a fresh certainty. Currently only confidence wording exists.

Deduplicate between '## What you know' and the crime role-directive sections — either suppress the top belief from summarizeForPrompt when the role builder already narrates it, or have the role builder reference 'the matter above' rather than re-stating who/what.

Fix verb framing per event: register phrasing per eventType/category (theft → 'stole from Y', attack → 'attacked Y') rather than one blanket 'committed {verb} against {target}'. The registry (registerBeliefPhrasing, event-registry.ts:762) already supports multiple functions with first-non-null-wins.
Replace the silent null-drop on unregistered event labels (beliefs.ts:132) with getEventLabelSafe-style fallback + warn, so 'known' beliefs cannot vanish from context unnoticed.

Guard recall against degenerate queries: skip vector recall (or widen to recent+important memories) when the query has <N meaningful tokens, instead of returning embedding noise or empty keyword results.

Consider feeding top recalled memories into the autonomous decision prompt (volition.ts) too, so lived experience influences actions, not just dialogue — or document the act-vs-speak split as intentional.

Add a soft token/char budget to buildSystemPrompt and order by importance so the memory block isn't the first casualty of truncation; alternatively move memories above the long Background/secret blocks.
When storing belief summaries as conversation memories (interaction.ts:112), tag them so recall can down-weight or exclude derived-from-belief entries, preventing the belief→memory→belief echo loop.

qualityRisks: No few-shot examples anywhere. A 9B model is told abstractly when to OMIT fields but never shown a concrete benign-message-with-empty-output example vs a threat example. extractionConfidence is self-assessed by the same model with zero rubric — no anchor for what 0.3 vs 0.8 means. It is clamped and defaulted to 0.5 (il.ts:266-267,299) but never actually gates anything downstream that I saw; likely decorative / low-trust signal.

On a stronger model (Claude) these crutches are harmless but the lack of examples + single-act constraint still caps quality. There is NO fallback route for IL, so any Qwen hiccup silently degrades every player utterance to 'smalltalk' with confidence 0 — a quiet, total loss of meaning with only a console.warn.

The full Known NPCs / locations / event types lists are dumped uncapped into a 400-token-output prompt every call. In a large world this (a) bloats the prompt and (b) gives a small model a long enum to mismatch against. No relevance filtering by who/what the player actually mentioned.

ctx.targetNpcId is threaded for per-NPC provider isolation, but IL is routed to LM Studio Qwen (shared, stateless) — the agentContext is effectively dead for this task, a latent mismatch if someone reroutes IL to claude-code expecting per-NPC memory.

Filter the injected NPC/location/event-type lists to entities plausibly relevant to the message (or at least cap + prioritize by recency/proximity) instead of dumping the full world every call — reduces prompt bloat and enum-mismatch surface for the 9B.

Define extractionConfidence with a 1-line rubric (e.g. 0.9 = explicit & unambiguous, 0.5 = inferred, 0.2 = guess) or drop it if nothing downstream gates on it — currently it is an ungrounded self-score.

Move the hardcoded trade categories ('weapon, armor, potion, food, general') into a registry (registerTradeCategories) to match the rest of the vocabulary-by-module pattern and avoid stale taxonomy.

crimeSeverity fallback is a magic 3 when no scene/belief match (step-handlers.ts:386) — a real crime with lost scene residue silently becomes 'moderate', narrowing available verdicts without the model knowing the data is degraded.

schemaInPrompt prompt-mode relies on extractJsonObject scraping the first balanced JSON object from free text; Sonnet emitting reasoning-then-JSON or fenced+prose can fail extraction → returns null → falls back to cold spawn (latency) or ultimately to lm-studio/qwen fallback which has weaker judgment for this high-value call.

REFLECTION output has no schema/validation at all — generate returns raw text; the only guard is a null→canned-string fallback ('Something has changed, but I cannot put it into words.'). Malformed or meta output ('Here is the insight:') is stored verbatim as a memory with importance 9.
REFLECTION instruction 'Respond with ONLY the insight, nothing else. No quotes, no prefixes.' is model-fragile — smaller fallback models (qwen) routinely add prefixes; no post-processing strips them.

TWO independent reflection mechanisms with overlapping intent (engine ReflectionTracker on importance>=50 storing to vector memory + reflections.md via hook, AND server consolidation of oldest-25 observations to reflections.md) — different prompts, different triggers, both append to reflections.md; risk of redundant/duplicate 'insights' and conceptual drift between the two.

Reflection memory list dumps RAW observation text with [importance: n] tags into the prompt — no de-duplication, so repeated similar observations skew the 'pattern' the model extracts toward whatever was most frequent rather than most significant.

Routing drift vs documentation: clwa/overview memory says reflection routes to lm-studio/qwen, but llm-defaults.ts:36 routes REFLECTION to claude-code/sonnet (warm) with qwen only as fallback — cost/latency assumptions in docs are stale.

Because verdict/reflection run as the NPC on claude-code, the ambient CLAUDE.md persona + 6 @memory files are injected but are INVISIBLE at the call site — the prompt author cannot see or control that context, and observations.md/reflections.md can grow unbounded between consolidations, ballooning per-call context and cost unpredictably.

VERDICT temperature 0.4 with reasoning required but no chain-of-thought scaffold: 'reasoning' is generated alongside the verdict in one shot, so it is post-hoc rationalization of the chosen enum rather than a deliberation that informs it.
improvementIdeas: Stop leaking guilt through buildSuspectDefense prose tone; either feed the model neutral defense facts and let it infer credibility, or explicitly separate 'observable demeanor' from a hidden guilt flag the model must not see.

Add the severity range to each AVAILABLE VERDICTS line (e.g. 'imprisonment: Temporary Imprisonment (severity 4-8, 2 days)') so the model can reason about proportionality the same way getAvailableVerdicts does.
Replace the single 'Consider:' rubric with 2-3 worked calibration examples (evidence profile + severity -> expected verdict) to anchor consistency across the 5 options.
Cap and rank evidence lines (e.g. top-N strong, then moderate, then weak) and surface the totalEvidence count + strongest-source label explicitly in the prompt, instead of only in console logs.
Make crimeSeverity fallback explicit to the model ('crime details degraded — severity estimated') rather than silently substituting 3, so the verdict can be appropriately cautious.
Give REFLECTION a tiny output schema or at least a post-processing strip of common prefixes/quotes, and validate non-empty before storing at importance 9.

Unify or clearly delineate the two reflection paths (threshold-based vector reflection vs observation consolidation) — e.g. have consolidation feed the same prompt template and de-dup against existing reflections to avoid drift.
De-duplicate / cluster the observation list before reflection so the extracted 'pattern' weights significance over frequency.
Reconcile llm-defaults.ts reflection route with the clwa/overview memory (or update the memory) — the doc/code disagreement risks wrong cost/latency reasoning in future work.

Surface (or budget) the ambient CLAUDE.md + @memory size for claude-code verdict/reflection calls, and ensure observations.md is consolidated before high-value verdict calls so per-call context stays bounded.
Bump or reconcile VERDICT maxTokens: route says 800 but call overrides to 300 with reasoning required — 300 tokens may truncate non-trivial reasoning; pick one intentional budget.

audit.limitsAndTruncation: Player history: _chatHistory hard-trimmed to last 12 messages (~6 exchanges) via slice(-12) (agent.ts:114-115); older turns are DROPPED with no summary. Memory recall: top-5 per turn (agent.ts:108,202). roleDirective beliefs: top-3 (summarizeForPrompt(3), agent.ts:368). serializeMemoryState beliefs: top-30 by confidence×recency (agent.ts:254) — Claude-provider projection only, not the local prompt. NPC↔NPC: only the single previous line carried forward (conversation.ts:266); full lines[] kept only for the event-store record. CONVERSATION_MAX_TOKENS=80 caps NPC↔NPC output; speech maxLength 80 chars. No relevance ranking on history (chronological FIFO trim).
qualityRisks: Lost history with no summary: player chat trims to last 12 messages (agent.ts:114) and there is NO rolling summary of dropped turns — anything said >6 exchanges ago vanishes from the conversational context entirely (only partially recoverable via the noisy top-5 vector memory recall).

clearChatHistory() (agent.ts:46) is DEFINED BUT NEVER CALLED anywhere in server or frontend (verified via grep). Its doc says 'called when player starts talking to a different NPC' — but it isn't, so a per-NPC buffer persists across separate conversations and only self-trims by count; switching away and back resumes stale mid-conversation context. Per-NPC buffer also lives only in process memory (not in save.json), so it silently resets on server restart.

Two divergent player paths: chat() (agent.ts:77, non-streaming) builds NO history and stores nothing in _chatHistory, while chatStream() (agent.ts:103) does. If any caller uses chat(), that NPC's multi-turn memory desyncs from the streaming path's buffer.

NPC↔NPC has near-zero history: buildFollowUpPrompt/buildResponderPrompt pass only the single immediately-preceding line (conversation.ts:266,255). In a multi-exchange conversation the model cannot see 2+ turns back — risk of topic drift, repetition, and contradiction; the explicit echo/repeat guards (conversation.ts:147,253) exist precisely because this is fragile.

Weak player-text framing: the raw player message is sent as the user turn with no 'The player/stranger says:' wrapper or identity context (unlike the NPC↔NPC responder prompt which quotes and attributes the speaker at conversation.ts:254). The NPC has no framed notion of WHO is speaking beyond relationship/trust directives, and the trade path mutates the user message with bracketed SHOP instructions (server.ts:303) that can leak as narration.

additionalContext is injected mid-prompt right before Rules (agent.ts:350), and the long system prompt has many ## sections before it — the code itself notes 'lost middle' causes the 9B to ignore mid-prompt context (server.ts:299), so trust/secret/IL directives risk being under-weighted.

Memory block and history can conflict: each turn injects the conversationText 'Player said: "...". I replied: "..."' into vector memory (agent.ts:133), so recalled memories may echo the same lines already in _chatHistory — duplication and possible self-reference reinforcement.

Speech-style example sampling (speechReminder, prompt-utils.ts:13) is random per call — non-deterministic voice cues turn to turn; combined with no few-shot dialogue examples, voice consistency relies entirely on prose description.

parseDialogue heuristics are fragile: the trailing-dash style-strip (conversation.ts:55-60) and curly/XML strippers are regex guesses that can truncate legitimate speech containing ' - ' or braces; only applies to NPC↔NPC (player free-text is unparsed/unsanitized).
No system/developer-role separation for Rules vs persona — everything is one system string; constraints like 'under 15 words' compete for attention with the entire personality/memory payload.
improvementIdeas: Actually call clearChatHistory() on NPC switch (frontend chat:open or server when msg.agentId changes) OR key history per-conversation; persist or explicitly document the in-memory-only nature in save.

Add a rolling summary of dropped turns: when slicing past 12 messages, condense the oldest pair into a compact 'Earlier you discussed X' line prepended to history, so >6-exchange context isn't lost (agent.ts:114).

For NPC↔NPC, pass a small history window (last 2-3 lines) into buildFollowUpPrompt/buildResponderPrompt instead of only the last line (conversation.ts:266), or thread an actual `history` array like the player path does.

Frame player text explicitly: wrap the user turn or add additionalContext naming the speaker and relationship ('A traveler you {trust label} is speaking to you'), so the NPC has a grounded interlocutor identity comparable to the NPC↔NPC responder prompt.
Unify the two player paths — make chat() delegate to the same history-aware buffer as chatStream(), or remove chat() if unused, to avoid desync.

Move the hard speech constraints (length, no-narration) into the user turn / a developer role near the end of context to dodge the documented 'lost middle' attenuation, rather than burying them after a long persona system prompt.

De-duplicate: skip injecting the literal 'Player said.../I replied...' memory while those turns are still in _chatHistory, or store a structured summary instead (mirrors the NPC↔NPC buildMemoryText no-raw-text approach at conversation.ts:285).
Make speechReminder example selection stable per conversation (seed once) to keep a consistent voice across turns.
Add 1-2 few-shot in-voice dialogue exemplars per NPC (or per archetype) to anchor style, reducing reliance on prose-only description.

keyPractices: Put the persona in the SYSTEM prompt, not the user turn. Anthropic: 'Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone... Even a single sentence makes a difference.' The system prompt is the persistent identity anchor; per-turn context goes in user messages.

Define the character densely, not abstractly. Anthropic keep-in-character: 'provide detailed information about the personality, background, and any specific traits or quirks. This will help the model better emulate and generalize the character's traits.' Include name/role, backstory, worldview/values, speech patterns + vocabulary, emotional triggers, hard behavioral constraints, and what the character does NOT know or do. Bare 'You are a knight' yields generic dialogue; specifics produce a voice.

Structure the persona with XML tags (<persona>, <values>, <speech_style>, <constraints>, <scenarios>) so Claude separates identity vs. rules vs. examples. Anthropic recommends consistent descriptive tag names; the mitigate-jailbreaks doc shows a real <values> block pattern.

Pre-load common scenarios with canned in-voice replies. Anthropic keep-in-character: 'Provide a list of common scenarios and expected responses... This trains Claude to handle diverse situations without breaking character.' Their AcmeBot example pairs trigger conditions with exact in-voice replies.

Use 3-5 few-shot examples to lock voice/tone, wrapped in <example>/<examples> tags. Anthropic: examples are 'one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output format, tone, and structure'; make them relevant, diverse (cover edge cases so Claude doesn't latch onto an unintended pattern), and structured. For dialogue, show full in-character turns including how the character handles being pushed off-topic.

Constrain output by SHOWING the format, not just describing it: 'Provide examples of your desired output. This trains Claude's understanding better than abstract instructions.' For strict-schema persona tasks prefer native Structured Outputs / tool-use enum over prose instructions.

Phrase constraints positively — tell Claude what TO do. Anthropic: instead of 'Do not use markdown' use 'compose your response in smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.' Add the WHY ('read aloud by TTS, so never use ellipses...'); Claude generalizes from the rationale. Positive examples beat negative instructions.

Counter the default assistant tone explicitly. Sonnet/Opus default to 'a direct, opinionated style with minimal validation-forward phrasing.' If your character is warmer/rougher/archaic, re-baseline ('Use a warm, collaborative tone' or specify exact register). Kill preambles/meta with 'Respond directly without preamble' + 'Never break character or refer to yourself as an AI/model/assistant.'

Author-framing > possession-framing for longer sessions. Community testing finds collaborative 'You are writing the character X who...' holds consistency better over long conversations than pure 'You ARE X' possession framing.

For long conversations, re-inject the persona via the USER turn (not prefill). Anthropic: prefill on the final assistant turn is REMOVED on Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.6+ (400 error). Official migration for 'role consistency': 'inject what were previously prefilled-assistant reminders into the user turn.' Prefill still works on Haiku 4.5 and older.

Tune effort + max_tokens for dialogue. Sonnet 4.6 defaults to effort=high; Anthropic recommends low (or medium) for chat 'For chat and non-coding use cases... start with low effort', thinking disabled if not needed, to cut latency/cost. Set a generous max_tokens so in-character replies aren't truncated.

Match prompt style to desired output style. Anthropic: 'removing markdown from your prompt can reduce the volume of markdown in the output.' For naturalistic spoken dialogue, write the system prompt in clean prose rather than dense markdown/bullets — formatting bleeds through.

Keep prompts short and high-signal, especially for Haiku. 'Longer, more complex prompts are NOT always better'; verbosity makes outputs worse. Trim persona to load-bearing traits + 3-5 examples rather than a lore wall.
applicabilityToCLWA: System-prompt design (all tasks): LlmCallRequest already separates `system` and `user`. Put the stable persona (NPC name, PM personality, Enneagram, speech register, hard constraints, 'never say you are an AI') in `system`; put volatile per-tick context (mood, beliefs, scene, instinct prose) in `user`. Matches Anthropic's role-in-system / context-in-user split and maximizes prompt-cache hits.

dialogue / npc-dialogue: canonical keep-in-character case. Dense <persona> + <speech_style> in system, 3-5 <example> dialogue turns showing voice and how the NPC deflects off-world/meta questions, explicit 'never break character, never reference being an AI/model.' Use author-framing; on long threads re-inject persona via the user turn (prefill is gone on Sonnet 4.6).

verdict / il / volition (structured tasks): use native Structured Outputs (json_schema) or tool-use enums, not prose persona tricks — Anthropic steers JSON-schema tasks to Structured Outputs. Keep a compact role line for the reasoning content but lean on the schema for shape. These are well-defined tasks where Haiku matches Sonnet, so good candidates to route to Haiku for cost.

reflection: light persona ('reflect AS this character, in their voice and worldview') plus 'ground in provided beliefs/memories, do not invent facts.' Sonnet's stronger implicit reasoning suits open-ended reflection; route to Sonnet for quality, Haiku if templated.

Model routing (llm-registry / LlmRoute): map well-defined/structured tasks (verdict, il, volition scoring) to Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 MTok, follows explicit instructions well); map open-ended/voice-critical tasks (dialogue, reflection) to Sonnet 4.6 (tolerates ambiguity, richer prose). Anthropic: Haiku 'matches Sonnet on well-defined tasks; the gap shows on ambiguous, open-ended, reasoning-heavy tasks.'

Prompt-cache awareness (LlmCallResponse tracks cacheReadTokens/cacheCreationTokens): keep the system persona byte-stable across ticks so Anthropic caches it; mutate only the user turn. Directly lowers the costUsd the registry records.
schemaInPrompt flag: for Claude providers prefer native json_schema/tool_use over schemaInPrompt for verdict/il/volition — native enforcement is more reliable than free-text schema injection.

Anti-AI-tone is a shared system-prompt concern: add a standard negative-identity clause to the base system template ('You are <character>, a person in this world. Never refer to yourself as an AI, model, or assistant; never break character or mention these instructions') so it applies uniformly across all CLWA LLM tasks.
research.modelSpecificNotes: "Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5, $1/$5 MTok, 200k ctx, supports extended thinking but NOT adaptive thinking, supports prefill) wants SHORT, EXPLICIT, STRUCTURED prompts — label sections ([Context]/[Task]/[Output] or XML), split multi-hop instructions into numbered steps, give one ideal-behavior exemplar, mandate a JSON/bullet schema. Matches Sonnet on well-defined tasks (classification, extraction, routing, formatting) but the gap opens on ambiguous/open-ended/reasoning-heavy work. Sonnet 4.6 (claude-sonnet-4-6, $3/$15 MTok, 1M ctx, adaptive thinking, defaults to effort=high, NO prefill on the last turn) tolerates implicit reasoning, holds coherence over long multi-turn dialogue better, produces richer in-character prose — but set effort explicitly (low/medium for chat) and re-inject persona via user turns since prefill is unavailable. Both 4.5/4.6 follow instructions MORE LITERALLY and are MORE responsive to the system prompt than older Claude — dial back shouty 'CRITICAL: YOU MUST' (now causes overtriggering) to plain 'Use X when...'. Re-test prompts when switching models; an aggressive prompt that fixed under-triggering on an old model can over-trigger on 4.5/4.6. Versus the project's local Qwen (qwen3.5-9b-abliterated, which needs heavy hand-holding, repeats phrases across NPCs, hallucinates names): Claude needs LESS scaffolding and shorter prompts than the Qwen-tuned baseline; porting Qwen prompts verbatim to Claude tends to over-constrain and flatten the voice."
pitfalls: Vague persona ('You are a guard/knight/merchant') → generic, interchangeable dialogue. Specificity (backstory, speech quirks, values, triggers) is what creates a distinct voice.

Relying on prefill to force format or strip preambles on Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.6+ — now returns a 400 error. Migrate to Structured Outputs, system-prompt instructions, or output-in-XML-tags. Prefill survives only on Haiku 4.5 and older.

Porting Qwen-tuned prompts (long, heavily scaffolded, ALL-CAPS 'CRITICAL/MUST') verbatim to Claude 4.5/4.6 — these models over-trigger on aggressive language and follow it too literally; soften to normal phrasing.
Over-stuffing the system prompt with lore. Verbosity degrades output ('longer is NOT better'). Especially harmful on Haiku. Keep persona load-bearing + 3-5 examples.
Negative-only instruction lists ('don't do X, don't do Y'). Claude steers better on positive instructions/examples; pair any 'don't' with the 'do' and a one-line rationale.

Forgetting to counter the default tone. Sonnet/Opus default to direct, low-validation, sparing-emoji prose; if your character is warm/florid/archaic/curt you must specify it or every NPC drifts toward the same neutral assistant register.
Letting the system prompt mutate every tick (kills prompt caching → higher costUsd). Keep the persona prefix byte-stable; vary only the user turn.
Homogeneous few-shot examples → Claude latches onto an unintended pattern. Examples must be diverse and cover edge cases (deflecting meta questions, hostility, silence).
Using schemaInPrompt / free-text schema for verdict/il/volition on Claude when native json_schema/tool_use is available — native enforcement is more reliable.
Not setting effort on Sonnet 4.6 (defaults to high) → unnecessary latency/cost on simple dialogue turns; and too-small max_tokens → truncated in-character replies.

Meta-leakage: without an explicit clause, Claude can slip into 'As an AI...', acknowledge the instructions, or break the fourth wall under adversarial input. Add an explicit never-break-character + never-self-identify-as-AI rule.

keyPractices: GROUNDING via atomic-fact verification (RoleFact): generate a draft reply, decompose it into atomic facts, check each fact against retrieved world facts (FCR). Keep a fact if the world-knowledge base supports it; drop it otherwise UNLESS the model's own confidence clears a calibrated threshold t (sample the self-check FCS m times, keep if k/m >= t). Then run a self-reflection rewrite (SRU) that removes all unsupported facts. This beat pure 'use only retrieved facts' (anonymizing the prompt) which HURT both informativeness AND factual precision — i.e. don't strip parametric knowledge entirely, modulate it. Result: +18% factual precision on adversarial Qs, -44% temporal hallucination.

KNOWLEDGE-BOUNDARY control via lightweight expert hints (TimeChara Narrative-Experts): before answering, a cheap pre-pass classifies the player's question and injects an explicit hint into the prompt. Temporal hint when the topic is in the NPC's future: 'Note that the period of the question is in the future relative to {character}'s time point. Therefore you should not answer or mention any facts that occurred after {character}'s time point.' Spatial hint when the NPC was not present at an event: 'Note that {character} had not participated in the scene described. Therefore do not imply {character} was present.' Even the zero-shot version of this instruction ('you should not answer or mention any fact future to the period; if not present at the location, the character is likely unaware') measurably cut hallucination.

PERSONA STABILITY: prefer a STATIC persona core over re-injecting persona every turn. The Fixed-Persona SLM paper bakes voice/temperament/knowledge-scope into the model (LoRA) so identity can't drift; CLWA's equivalent (no fine-tuning) is a short, fixed persona block placed FIRST and unchanged across turns, with only memory/world facts varying. Persona drift is measurable: self-consistency degrades >30% after ~8-12 turns even with intact context, so don't rely on a one-time system prompt for long sessions.

KEEP THE SYSTEM PROMPT SHORT (<300 tokens target). LLMs weight instructions, not read them linearly; buried directives in 800+ token walls get deprioritized. Repeat the few load-bearing constraints at the BEGINNING and END — the last message before generation gets disproportionate attention (use it for the critical 'reply in 1-2 sentences, in-character, only known facts' guard).

DESCRIBE ACTIONS, DON'T NEGATE TRAITS. Put desired emotional/behavioral patterns into the persona as identity/backstory and concrete behaviors ('keeps hands loose at her sides', 'answers curtly when suspicious') rather than rules like 'NEVER show shame' — negations are weak and flip-flop. Use natural-language skill/trait rubrics ('nimble', 'graceful', 'wary') instead of bare numbers; the LLM interprets words better than scores.

EMOTION/MOOD via mood-dependent retrieval (Emotional RAG): retrieve memories using BOTH semantic similarity AND emotional-state similarity to the NPC's current mood (combination or sequential strategy). Reinstating the original emotion at recall keeps personality coherent. Pairs naturally with CLWA's mood value — bias memory retrieval toward memories tagged with the current mood, and state the current mood explicitly in the prompt so it colors tone.

COLLABORATIVE / AUTHOR FRAMING beats 'You ARE X'. Either (a) frame as a skilled author voicing the character, or (b) wrap player input as attributed speech ('Player says: ...') and have the LLM continue the scene. Both reduce the drift toward generic assistant tone and handle edge cases more gracefully. Add explicit anti-assistant guards: never break the fourth wall, never add moral disclaimers, end at a natural beat, don't end every reply with a question.

MATCH PACING / CONCISION: instruct the NPC to mirror the player's register — short punchy player line gets a short reply. Between turns, do light editorial compression of idle chatter so context stays on-point. This keeps replies natural rather than the LLM's default verbose paragraph.

MEMORY ARCHITECTURE: two decoupled stores (per Fixed-Persona SLM + Generative Agents). (1) Conversation memory = prior turns for continuity; (2) World-knowledge memory = structured in-universe facts the NPC may know. Query each independently by cosine similarity, take top-k, concatenate into the prompt. Cap raw history (the cross-platform NPC paper uses a 6-round window) and use guided summarization to compress older turns (Bicking) rather than unbounded context. Generative Agents rank memories by recency + importance + relevance and add periodic Reflection (synthesize higher-level beliefs) — maps to CLWA reflection/belief tasks.

VERIFY/MEASURE with adversarial tests: build a small eval set of (a) cross-universe questions an NPC shouldn't answer, (b) future/not-present questions, (c) open-ended questions (to confirm the NPC didn't become over-conservative and refuse everything). Use an LLM-as-judge for factual correctness AND appropriate refusal. RoleFact/TimeChara both show refusal-quality and over-conservatism must be measured together, not just hallucination.

SMALL-MODEL DATA QUALITY > QUANTITY: for local fine-tuned personas, a curated ~115-pair seed beat a ~564-pair synthetic set on factuality and retention (overfitting/noise). If CLWA ever LoRA-tunes Qwen personas, prioritize a small hand-reviewed dataset; the paper's best config was Mistral-7B-Instruct + small dataset (93% factuality, 100% context retention).
applicabilityToCLWA: dialogue (general LLM dialogue task): Adopt a fixed, FIRST-position persona block + the RoleFact draft->decompose->verify-against-world-facts->rewrite loop as an optional post-pass for high-stakes lines; at minimum add the TimeChara-style explicit knowledge-boundary sentence to the system prompt ('only state facts you actually know from your memory/beliefs; if unsure, say you don't know rather than invent names or events'). Keep the system prompt <300 tokens and restate the 1-2-sentence + in-character + known-facts-only guard at the very end of the prompt.

npc-dialogue: Use the two-store memory split already implied by npc-memory-manager.ts — conversation memory (recent turns, ~6-round window) + world/belief facts — retrieved top-k and injected, with the player's line wrapped as attributed speech ('{player} says: ...') to anchor in-character continuation. Bias world-fact retrieval to the speaking NPC's beliefs only (their knowledge boundary), preventing one NPC from voicing facts only another NPC knows — directly addresses the name-hallucination limitation noted in CLWA memory.

npc-dialogue (name hallucination specifically): enforce that any proper noun in the reply must appear in the retrieved facts/beliefs context; the RoleFact atomic-fact check on 'name-only third-person' facts is the principled version. Cheaper heuristic for Qwen: a post-generation pass that flags reply tokens looking like names not present in the injected context and asks for a rewrite.

verdict / reflection: TimeChara's decomposed-reasoning and Generative-Agents Reflection map onto CLWA's verdict and reflection tasks — keep the reasoning/judgment step SEPARATE from the surface dialogue step (decomposed experts > one monolithic prompt), and let reflection synthesize higher-level beliefs that then become retrievable world-facts for future dialogue grounding.

volition / il (internal layer): use Bicking's hidden internal-monologue technique — generate the NPC's private thought/intent first (never shown), then the spoken line. This gives volition/il a coherent motivation to surface in dialogue and improves consistency without exposing reasoning to the player.

Emotional expression across tasks: feed CLWA's mood value into BOTH retrieval (Emotional RAG mood-dependent recall) and the prompt (state current mood explicitly), and express mood through described behavior/tone in the persona rather than negation rules. The VER paper's turn-level + dialogue-level emotion alignment is the eval target if measuring emotional drift.

System-prompt design (global): centralize the shared guard rails (anti-assistant, anti-fourth-wall, concision, known-facts-only, action-not-negation) in llm-defaults.ts as a compact reusable block; keep per-NPC persona in the character/world config (millhaven world.json), and DO NOT duplicate or contradict facts between the global block and per-NPC card — conflicting fields cause flip-flopping.
research.modelSpecificNotes: "Claude (Sonnet/Haiku, CLWA's claude-code provider): strong enough to follow author-framing, the explicit knowledge-boundary sentence, and the RoleFact self-check/rewrite loop in-context without fine-tuning; can run the atomic-fact decomposition + verification as extra LLM calls when latency budget allows. Best ROI: tight <300-token system block + TimeChara hint sentence + restating the concision/known-facts guard at prompt end. Haiku is cheap enough to act as the FCR/FCS fact-checker or the name-hallucination post-pass over Qwen-generated drafts. Small local models (Qwen on the RTX 3080): the literature (Fixed-Persona SLM, TimeChara baselines with Mistral-7B) shows 7B-class models hold persona FAR better when the identity is baked in (LoRA) or kept in a SHORT fixed prefix than when relying on long instructions they deprioritize. Qwen will (a) drift to assistant tone faster, (b) hallucinate names/facts more, (c) ignore buried rules — so for Qwen: shorten the prompt aggressively, put the one critical constraint LAST, prefer concrete behavior descriptions over abstract rules, cap history to ~6 turns + summarize, and lean on retrieval grounding (only known facts in context) rather than trusting parametric knowledge. Mistral-7B-Instruct with a small curated LoRA hit 93% factuality / 100% context retention locally on 8GB VRAM (~5.5s latency, masked by streaming/TTS) — a realistic target if CLWA ever fine-tunes personas; note quantization (GPTQ) there caused severe latency (35s) for marginal disk savings, so avoid aggressive quant on the 3080 unless VRAM-bound. Cross-NPC phrase repetition (a known CLWA Qwen issue) aligns with persona-drift findings — mitigate with distinct fixed persona prefixes per archetype and mood-varied retrieval rather than identical prompts."
pitfalls: Stripping parametric knowledge entirely (forcing 'use ONLY retrieved facts'): RoleFact showed anonymizing prompts to kill parametric knowledge LOWERED both informativeness and factual precision. Modulate, don't amputate — allow confident parametric facts, only delete unsupported ones.

Over-conservatism: aggressive hallucination guards make the NPC refuse or hedge on everything, killing immersion. Always co-measure refusal quality on open-ended questions, not just hallucination on adversarial ones (RoleFact's OEI task exists precisely for this).

Walls of instructions: 800+ token system prompts cause the model (especially small local ones) to deprioritize buried rules. The single most important constraint must be short and placed at the prompt's end.
Re-injecting / mutating the persona every turn invites drift and contradicts itself; keep the persona core static and only vary memory/mood/facts.
Conflicting fields across system prompt vs. character card vs. world config — the model 'flip-flops unpredictably'. De-duplicate; one source of truth per fact.
Negation-based emotion rules ('NEVER show shame', 'do not be robotic') are weak; models comply unreliably. Use positive concrete behavior descriptions instead.

Reusing identical prompts across model families/instances — GLM/Llama/Claude/Qwen respond differently, and identical prompts across NPCs cause cross-NPC phrase repetition. Tune per model; differentiate per NPC.
Assuming bigger fine-tuning data is better: for LoRA personas, larger synthetic datasets OVERFIT and degraded factuality vs. a small curated set.
Letting raw conversation history grow unbounded: dilutes memory and bloats context. Cap the window (~6 rounds) and summarize older turns.

Ending every reply with a question or breaking the fourth wall with disclaimers — classic assistant tells that destroy the in-character illusion; explicitly forbid and instruct to end on a natural story beat.

Trusting an NPC to respect its own knowledge boundary implicitly — it won't. Without an explicit temporal/spatial 'you don't know X' hint and grounding to that NPC's own beliefs, NPCs voice future events and other characters' private knowledge.

keyPractices: Score memories on a weighted composite, not pure vector similarity. The canonical Stanford generative-agents formula is score = recency + importance + relevance with each term min-max normalized to [0,1] and all weights = 1; recency is exponential decay (their factor 0.995 per game-hour since last RETRIEVAL, not since creation), importance is an LLM-assigned 1-10 'mundane-to-poignant' score, relevance is embedding cosine. CLWA already does this (memory.ts recall: relevance*0.4 + decayedImportance*0.4 + freshness*0.2) — the practice is sound; the tunable gap is that CLWA's recency keys off creation day, not last-access, so frequently-recalled memories don't stay warm.

Over-fetch then rerank. Retrieve a wide candidate set by cheap similarity (CLWA does topK*3), then re-rank by the full composite and slice to a small final K. This is exactly the right pattern; the only refinement is to make the final injected K small (5-8) because every extra memory dilutes attention.

Put the most load-bearing context at the START and END of the window, never the middle. Liu et al. measured 30%+ accuracy loss when the key document moves to the middle of a 20-doc context; the curve is U-shaped (primacy+recency) and is an architectural artifact of RoPE. Practically: stable persona/instructions first, then mid-priority memory, then the single most decision-relevant item (current dialogue turn / top belief) LAST, immediately before the model speaks.

Order retrieved memories by ascending relevance so the highest-scored item lands closest to the question (end position). Putting your best-ranked memory in the middle of a long beliefs block wastes it.

Separate stable persona (system) from volatile state (per-turn). Persona/personality/secret = write once, cache; mood/location/relationships/beliefs = refresh each call. CLWA's split (CLAUDE.local.md persona written once + per-call snapshotState rewriting current-state/relationships/beliefs) is textbook-correct and also a prompt-caching win.

Compact long history rather than truncating it. Summarize old turns/observations into 1-2 sentence high-fidelity insights; mem0 reports up to 80% token reduction with preserved fidelity. CLWA's consolidateObservations (LLM-distill oldest 25 obs -> one reflection line, keep recent 25) and ReflectionTracker (importance-threshold-triggered epiphany) implement this correctly.

Compact PROACTIVELY, not at the limit. Context-rot research: reactive compaction at ~95% capacity is too late — degraded outputs already happened. Trigger consolidation on a budget threshold (e.g. 70-80%) or on entry count, which CLWA's count-based trigger (keepRecent+consolidateOldest) approximates.

Treat the window as a hard token budget and curate 'the smallest set of high-signal tokens.' Reserve explicit budget per section (persona N, beliefs M, dialogue history K) and enforce caps; more context does not monotonically improve quality (context rot affects every frontier model at every length increment).

Prefer structured/delimited context over prose for state. Use Markdown headers / XML tags to delineate sections (Anthropic) and structured fields (typed sentiment 0.62 + label '(friendly)') for state. CLWA's renderers (numeric value + human label) hit the sweet spot: machine-precise yet salient to the LLM.

Promote to long-term memory selectively. Don't store everything — let the agent reflect and assign an importance/usefulness score before persisting; retire by recency + retrieval-frequency. CLWA does importance-gated storage + capacity eviction by decayedImportance with a 'protected' immunity flag — exactly this.

Just-in-time / hybrid retrieval. Keep lightweight identifiers and pull data into context at runtime via tools rather than pre-loading everything; use a hybrid (some up front for speed + on-demand pull). CLWA's @memory/*.md imports refreshed per call are a pre-load model; the JIT upgrade is to recall only memories relevant to the CURRENT topic/interlocutor rather than a fixed top-30.

Feed tool/parse errors back into context. LLMs are good at reading error messages and self-correcting; surface failed-call errors instead of masking them (CLWA's parseDialogue already refuses to fake a fallback on empty LLM output, logging upstream — keep that discipline).

Beware the four failure modes when stuffing memory: poisoning (a wrong belief persists and compounds), distraction (too many low-value memories), confusion (irrelevant retrievals), and clash (contradictory memories in-context). Confidence-decayed beliefs and dedup/merge logic mitigate these.
applicabilityToCLWA: npc-dialogue / conversation.ts threading: The U-shape rule is the highest-impact change. buildResponderPrompt/buildFollowUpPrompt put the interlocutor's last line near the top then trail with voice/mood reminders — but the model speaks AFTER reading the whole persona system prompt. Move the single most decision-relevant token block (the line being reacted to + the active topic) to the very END of the user turn, and keep persona cached at the very start. Also: dialogue history is currently re-summarized into structured memory (buildMemoryText) rather than threaded verbatim — good for avoiding self-reference cascade, but for multi-turn coherence consider threading the last 1-2 verbatim lines at the END position only.

beliefs injection (renderBeliefs / snapshotState 'top-30'): top-30 by composite is likely too many for a small local model and lands mid-context. Reduce to top 5-8, and select beliefs relevant to the current interlocutor/topic (JIT) instead of a global top-N. Place the beliefs block late in the @memory ordering, and within it sort ascending so the strongest belief is last.

memory.ts recall composite: weights (0.4/0.4/0.2) are reasonable but diverge from the Stanford equal-weight baseline; the bigger fix is recency-on-last-access vs recency-on-creation, and min-max normalizing the three terms per query (currently decayedImportance is divided by 10 in decay.ts compositeScore but the live recall path in memory.ts uses raw decayedImportance un-normalized — a real inconsistency worth reconciling).

reflection.ts / consolidateObservations: correct compaction pattern; tune to trigger proactively on token/entry budget rather than only on cumulative-importance threshold (50). Reflections get importance 9 and thus dominate recall — verify that's intended (it makes epiphanies sticky, which is good, but can crowd out fresh observations).

system-prompt design (llm-npc-prompt-builder.ts buildNpcSystemPrompt): well-calibrated 'altitude' — concrete personality numbers + heuristic prose, sectioned with Markdown headers. Persona-in-system + state-in-@memory separation is the right stable/volatile split and is prompt-cache friendly. Keep the persona stable (write-once) so the cache prefix stays warm across calls.

verdict / il / volition / reflection LLM tasks: these consume the same per-call snapshot files; apply identical rules — small curated belief/memory set, structured fields with labels, critical instruction (the JSON schema / decision criterion) placed LAST in the user turn, and the persona cached first.
research.modelSpecificNotes: CLWA runs a small local model (qwen3.5-9b-abliterated via LM Studio), which changes the cost/benefit sharply versus Claude Sonnet/Haiku. (1) Effective working context is much smaller in practice — small models suffer lost-in-the-middle and context rot earlier and harder, so aggressive curation (top 5-8 memories, not 30) matters MORE than on frontier models. (2) Instruction-following under long system prompts is weaker — this is why conversation.ts had to inject the DIALOGUE rule into additionalContext 'so it gets equal attention weight with personality'; that workaround is exactly the right instinct (re-state critical constraints near the decision point / end). (3) Structured-output adherence (the strict JSON DIALOGUE_SCHEMA, maxLength 80) is more fragile on a 9B model — hence the extensive defensive parseDialogue cleanup (tag/brace/style-leak stripping). On Claude that defensiveness would be largely unnecessary; on Qwen it's load-bearing. (4) Prompt caching: Claude offers explicit cache_control for the stable persona prefix (big win given write-once CLAUDE.local.md); LM Studio's KV-cache reuse is more implicit, so keeping the persona byte-identical across calls is what preserves any reuse. (5) Importance scoring: Stanford used an LLM to assign 1-10 importance; on a small local model that call is noisy and cheap-but-unreliable, so CLWA's structured/topic-weight-derived importance (estimateImportance from topic.weight) is a sensible, more deterministic substitute. (6) Reranking: small models benefit most from over-fetch-then-rerank because they cannot themselves 'distill relevance autonomously' from a long dump the way Anthropic says frontier models can — so do the relevance filtering OUTSIDE the model, which CLWA does.
pitfalls: Injecting too many memories/beliefs (CLWA's top-30) — dilutes attention, increases cost, and on a 9B model actively degrades coherence. More context is not better.
Placing the most important item in the MIDDLE of a long block (30%+ accuracy loss). Never bury the active dialogue line or top belief between persona and trailing reminders.
Recency keyed off creation time instead of last-access — long-relevant memories that keep getting recalled go stale and get evicted; defeats the purpose of recency weighting.

Inconsistent normalization: decay.ts compositeScore divides decayedImportance by 10, but memory.ts recall multiplies raw decayedImportance — the two code paths score differently. Reconcile and min-max normalize per query (Stanford does this so the three terms are comparable).
Truncating history instead of summarizing it — loses information silently. CLWA avoids this via consolidation; don't regress to hard truncation under time pressure.
Reactive compaction at the capacity ceiling — by the time you hit ~95% the outputs are already degraded. Compact on a lower budget threshold.
Letting reflections (importance 9) permanently crowd out fresh observations in recall — sticky epiphanies are good, but verify the eviction/decay balance so the agent still notices new events.

Context poisoning: a single wrong high-confidence belief persists and compounds across turns; rely on confidence decay + evidence-based reinforcement, and don't store unverified inferences as high-importance.

Mixing volatile state into the cached persona prompt — any per-call change (mood, location) inserted into the system prefix breaks prompt caching and forces full re-encode. Keep persona byte-stable; state goes only in the refreshed @memory files.

Dumping raw prose conversation transcripts into memory creates a self-reference cascade (NPCs echoing prior phrasing — a known CLWA limitation). CLWA's buildMemoryText already stores structured topic+tone+belief summaries instead of verbatim lines; keep it that way.
Bloated/overlapping tool or instruction sets — Anthropic warns clarity beats coverage; for CLWA keep each LLM task's instruction set minimal and the JSON schema strict.

keyPractices: Pin the schema with native constrained decoding, not prose alone. LM Studio already sends response_format: json_schema with strict:true — keep it ON for every Qwen structured task. Benchmarks: prompt-only JSON scored <40% on complex schemas vs ~100% with structured outputs; one team cut post-processing errors 32%→0.4%. This makes hallucinated keys and unclosed brackets mathematically impossible, which is exactly the 7-9B failure class.

Order schema fields so reasoning comes BEFORE the decision. Put any free-text 'reason'/'rationale' field first and the enum/verdict field LAST. Autoregressive models condition the final answer on tokens already emitted — emitting the verdict first then justifying it is post-hoc rationalization and measurably worse. This is the cheap substitute for chain-of-thought under a strict schema.

Constrain values to short, descriptive enums — never free strings where a choice exists. Aidan Cooper: forcing a model onto 'esoteric' or unnatural tokens (e.g. lowercased labels) lowers confidence and accuracy; use natural, descriptive enum members that match how the model would phrase them. For CLWA volition this means the affordance-id list should read naturally, not as opaque codes.

Keep one or two worked examples INLINE in the system prompt for small models, even though you skip them for Sonnet. Few-shot reliably lifts small/instruction-tuned models on format and edge cases (omitted optional fields, null handling). Frontier models get this zero-shot; Qwen needs the demonstration. Pick examples that show the tricky cases (a null, a 'do nothing', a refusal) — not the happy path.

Match temperature to task TYPE, and never use greedy (temp 0) on Qwen. Qwen3-class explicitly degrades / repeats under greedy decoding — use sampling. Structured/deterministic tasks: ~0.15-0.4 with top_p~0.8, top_k~20 (CLWA's il=0.15, volition=0.35 are well-placed). Roleplay/dialogue: 0.7-1.0. Add presence_penalty ~0.5-1.5 only for roleplay to kill repetition (warning: >1.0 can cause language-mixing on Qwen).

Write SHORT, DIRECT, imperative instructions for the portable prompt; sophistication actively hurts small models. MePO finding: prompts optimized for frontier models exploit abstract multi-step reasoning that 7-9B models cannot execute, degrading quality. Portable-prompt merits = simplicity, explicit concrete guidance, task-aligned vocabulary, moderate length. One verb-led instruction per line beats a paragraph.

Send ONLY task-relevant context — trim aggressively. Context rot degrades 7-9B retrieval at every length increase, not just mid-context; padding 'just in case' is net-negative. For volition, feed only the scored affordance shortlist + current mood/relationship facts that bear on the choice, not the full world state.

Re-inject the critical constraint near the END of the prompt (recency / 'Forget-Me-Not'). Small models suffer instruction attenuation — a rule stated only once at the top gets ignored after long context. Restate the single hardest rule (e.g. 'Output ONLY the JSON object, no prose') as the last line.

Always validate + cheap-retry; treat structured output as best-effort even with strict schemas. CLWA already does truncateToFirstJsonObject — keep a schema-validate step and on failure do a one-shot reformat retry (or fall back to a stricter sampler). Never trust the first parse downstream.

Do NOT mix a long chain-of-thought INTO the schema for small models. Combining verbose reasoning + strict structure in one object conflicts with how models separate 'instructions' from 'values' and reduces accuracy. Prefer one short reason field (see field-order practice) over a multi-step scratchpad embedded in JSON; if you need real CoT, do it in a separate unconstrained call then format in a second call.
applicabilityToCLWA: volition (Qwen, temp 0.35, json_schema, maxTokens 100): This is a constrained CHOICE task — ideal for structured outputs. Make the affordance list a natural-language enum, put a one-line 'reason' field before the chosen 'action' field, and feed only the scored shortlist (already utility-pre-filtered by PM, per CLAUDE.md 'PM=instinct, LLM=consciousness'). 100 tokens is tight — keep the reason field to one short sentence so the JSON never truncates. Add a 1-shot example showing a 'wait/do-nothing' pick so Qwen learns it may decline.

il / interpretation layer (Qwen, temp 0.15, json_schema, maxTokens 400): Lowest temperature = most deterministic; good for extraction-style work, but 0.15 is near-greedy — confirm sampling stays enabled (LM Studio passes temperature, not greedy, so OK). This is the task most exposed to OVER-EXTRACTION: instruct it to populate only fields with explicit evidence and emit null otherwise (matches INV-07 null=unknown). One example demonstrating a null/absent field will cut invented values more than any wording change.

embeddings (nomic-embed via LM Studio, Matryoshka 768): No prompting concern — but note the raw-fetch path exists specifically to avoid SDK truncation of 768→192. The cross-model-comparison takeaway: embeddings are model-locked, so any Qwen→Claude comparison must hold the embedding model constant or memory-retrieval differences will confound the LLM comparison.

verdict (Sonnet primary, Qwen fallback temp 0.4, schemaInPrompt, maxTokens 300): This is the clearest graceful-degradation case in the codebase. Write ONE prompt that: (a) states the rule set as short imperative lines, (b) uses reason-before-verdict field order, (c) carries an inline example that you can leave in for both tiers (Sonnet ignores the redundancy cheaply, Qwen needs it). The Qwen fallback gets only 300 tokens vs Sonnet's 800 — design the schema so the minimum-viable verdict fits in 300.

reflection (Sonnet primary, Qwen fallback temp 0.7, maxTokens 150): Creative-leaning, short. Temp 0.7 is right for the fallback. Known limitation (from memory): cross-NPC phrase repetition — mitigate on the Qwen path with a small presence_penalty (~0.5) and by injecting the NPC's recent reflection lines as 'avoid repeating these' context.

npc-dialogue (Qwen primary, temp 0.7, maxTokens 200): Pure roleplay on the small model. Persona drift and name hallucination (a noted CLWA limitation) are the risks. Mitigate with a tight character block (name, traits, speaking style, current mood/relationship) restated compactly, recency re-injection of the persona rule at prompt end, and constraining referenced entities to an explicit roster so Qwen can't invent names. EVA-Qwen experience shows 7B holds persona for dozens of turns when the character card is concrete.

System-prompt design (cross-cutting): Author the portable prompt to the SMALL model's ceiling and let frontier models coast. Short imperative rules + inline example + reason-before-answer schema + end-of-prompt constraint re-injection is a single template that works on Qwen and is harmless on Haiku/Sonnet. Avoid frontier-only devices (deep multi-step CoT in the prompt, abstract meta-instructions) — they tank Qwen while barely helping Sonnet.

Cross-model comparison goal: To compare Qwen vs Haiku vs Sonnet fairly on the SAME task, hold everything constant except the model: same json_schema (strict), same inline example, same field order, same trimmed context, and log schema-validation pass rate + retry count as a first-class metric. Differences in raw format-failure rate are largely erased by constrained decoding, so the comparison should focus on DECISION QUALITY (does volition pick the in-character action?) not format compliance.
research.modelSpecificNotes: Frontier (Claude Sonnet/Haiku): Reliable zero-shot instruction following; handle long multi-step instructions and abstract framing; tolerate redundant inline examples cheaply; produce schema-valid JSON at high rates even prompt-only. They can do reasoning-then-answer implicitly. Risk profile skews to sycophancy and verbosity rather than format breakage. In CLWA they sit on warm sessions (dialogue/verdict/reflection) where latency, not format reliability, is the constraint. — Small/local (Qwen 7-9B): Need explicit demonstrations (few-shot) for edge cases; degrade under instruction-heavy/abstract prompts (MePO); suffer instruction attenuation, context rot, over-extraction, persona drift, name hallucination, and repetition/mode-collapse. Must NOT use greedy decoding (Qwen3-class repeats/breaks). Benefit disproportionately from native constrained decoding — it lifts a 7-9B model toward frontier-level format reliability, which is the single highest-leverage intervention. Key asymmetry: a prompt tuned for Sonnet often fails on Qwen, but a prompt tuned for Qwen (short, explicit, exampled, schema-pinned, reason-before-answer) runs fine on Sonnet — so author to the small model. Sampling differs by mode: Qwen non-thinking ~temp 0.7/top_p 0.8/top_k 20; thinking-mode ~temp 0.6/top_p 0.95; structured ~0.15-0.4. Roleplay tolerates presence_penalty for anti-repetition where structured tasks should not use it.
pitfalls: Relying on prose-only 'respond in JSON' instructions for Qwen — measured <40% adherence on complex schemas; always pair with the native json_schema constraint CLWA already has.
Using greedy decoding / temperature 0 on Qwen for determinism — it makes output WORSE (repetition, getting stuck). Use low-temp sampling (0.15-0.4) instead.

Setting max_tokens too low for a structured call — truncates the JSON mid-object and causes parse failure. CLWA's volition (100) and verdict-fallback (300) caps are tight; design schemas to fit or the strict parser fails. Alibaba explicitly warns against constraining max_tokens on JSON tasks.
Emitting the decision/enum field BEFORE the rationale field — yields post-hoc rationalization and worse decisions on small models. Always reason-then-answer in field order.
Forcing the model onto unnatural/esoteric enum values (opaque codes, forced lowercasing) — lowers token confidence and accuracy; use natural descriptive labels.

Porting a frontier-tuned, instruction-heavy prompt down to Qwen unchanged — verbose multi-step instructions overwhelm 7-9B and degrade quality (downward-compatibility problem). Don't 'just point the same prompt at the small model.'

Embedding a long chain-of-thought scratchpad inside the strict JSON schema — mixing reasoning and values in one structured object reduces accuracy on small models; keep one short reason field or split into two calls.
Stating the critical rule only once at the top of a long prompt — instruction attenuation means Qwen ignores it later; re-inject at the end.
Padding the prompt with 'might be useful' world context — context rot degrades small-model retrieval at every length increase. Trim to task-relevant facts only (acute for volition/il).

Trusting structured output without validation+retry — even strict decoding can mis-fill enums or emit empty objects; over-extraction (inventing fields/values) still happens on il-style tasks. Keep schema validation + one reformat retry.

Comparing Qwen vs Claude on a metric (format-failure rate) that constrained decoding flattens — you'll conclude 'they're equal' when the real differences are in decision/roleplay quality. Measure the right thing.

Cranking presence/repetition penalty high on Qwen to fix repetition — >1.0 risks language-mixing and quality drops; use modest values and only on roleplay/reflection paths, never on strict structured tasks.
